utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, if you have other business, Mr. President, you could certainly proceed. I just wanted to have one minute of the Chamber's time, please, before the witness is brought in. But I can take it in any order if you would like to -- if you have something else to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's some administrative matters I would like to say before I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Trial Chamber heard arguments of both parties with regard to the time schedule problem for this week caused by Mr. Naletilic's dentist appointment on Thursday, 27th, September at 11.00 a.m. The Trial Chamber accepts the dental treatment of Mr. Naletilic is of a certain urgency, and he should be enable to see the dentist on Thursday. The Trial Chamber ordered the registrar to look into the allegations that Mr. Naletilic has not been provided with pain killing medication for a certain period and report back to the Trial Chamber. The registrar is further called upon by the Trial Chamber to adequately monitor and ensure the further treatment of Mr. Naletilic's teeth problems. Lastly, the Trial Chamber asks the registrar to keep in mind the Court schedule of this Trial Chamber. If the scheduling of any further medical appointments should become necessary, such appointments should, in general, be scheduled before and after the regular sitting hours, which are 9.30 a.m. and 4 p.m., and on Friday afternoon after 1.00 p.m. As to Defence argument that the trial cannot commence in the absence of Mr. Naletilic, the Trial Chamber wishes to point out very clearly that generally, this Trial Chamber holds the view that short-term absence of the accused does not prevent the Trial Chamber from commencing the trial, provided that the accused is represented by the counsel during his absence. In this regard, the Trial Chamber will not allow the delay of a trial by medical appointments that may become necessary or desirable. It is only for the particular circumstances of Mr. Naletilic's treatment this week and the special importance of the witness to be heard that the Trial Chamber, nevertheless, grants the motion of the accused, that the trial will not be commenced during his absence on Thursday morning. Due to the oft-discussed particular circumstances in this trial week, the Trial Chamber decided to sit on Thursday and Friday as follows: On Thursday, September 27th, we will sit only in the afternoon from 2.00 p.m. until 5:30 p.m. On Friday, September 28th, we will sit during the regular court hours for the morning session, and in addition, from 2.30 to 5.30 p.m., if this will become necessary to complete the Prosecution's witnesses for this week. As for the second week of October, as already announced earlier this week, Trial Chamber 1, Section A, will not sit in the first week of October. Due to additional professional obligations of the Judges, the Trial Chamber will sit in the second week of October only, from Monday morning, October 8th, until and including Thursday morning, October 11th. The Trial Chamber will not sit on Thursday afternoon and on Friday morning, October 12th. The trial will resume on October 15th, 2001, with the normal court hours. This Trial Chamber will also not sit on October 24th, because that is a UN holiday. And yesterday, at the end of the afternoon session, Mr. Meek raised an issue of the search and the seizure warrant. Due to the tight time schedule of the rest of this week, we will not discuss this issue any further in the Court at this point since it has, however, not become entirely clear to the Trial Chamber what kind of relief the Defence is actually requiring. We request Mr. Meek to file a written explanation of your request and file it according to the rules for filing documents in this case. Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, did you talk to your witness yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I talked to him in the morning. It was a very brief conversation, mostly about the problems of behaviour in the courtroom and the manner of answering questions to both parties, to the Prosecutor and to the Defence. It seems to me that Witness U understood that he should behave himself properly here in the courtroom, and I hope that today's session with this witness can be shorter. The Defence will, of course...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think all of us -- at least me, have to get used to the adversary systems in this courtroom, including your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: With regard to the afternoon session, the Trial Chamber wishes to express the following, because unfortunately, it seems to me I have to remind counsel of their professional duties in general, and specifically with the Trial Chamber's order with the questioning of witnesses which was issued orally at the beginning of this trial. Once again, the Trial Chamber requests the parties to put all questions to the witness in a short and direct way. This Trial Chamber will attach only little evidential weight to answers that result from any kind of suggestive questions. Suggestive questions are such that consist only of a simple confirmation of the suggested answer that has been given to the witness by the questioning parties themselves. This Trial Chamber will further not tolerate any longer any discussion between counsel and the witnesses in the courtroom. It is the professional duty of the party who calls the witness to ensure that the witness fully understands that his function in the courtroom is to give his evidence to the Trial Chamber and that he is not allowed to enter into inquiries with the questioning party. At the same time, it is the professional duty of the questioning party in the court to prevent such debates instead of contributing further to it. Lastly, the Trial Chamber once again calls upon the parties to pay due respect to witnesses during the questioning and to act like professional counsel in this regard. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, we appreciate all that information very much, especially concerning scheduling. So it assists us, obviously, in planning, and we thank the Court for that information. In that same regard, I just want to alert the Court - and again for witness scheduling reasons - if the cross-examination of this first witness is not completed by the 11.00 break, and again I'm not meaning to exert any pressure on the cross-examination of the witness but only as a scheduling matter, we would propose to the Chamber that if we're not finished by 11.00, that at the 11.30 time, when we resume at 11.30, that we be able to take the next witness out of order, who will be a very short witness, we think, and we can complete that witness in a very short time, we think, and allow that person to actually leave The Hague today. The realities are, as I understand them with the witness that's presently testifying, that because of the airline schedules to Bosnia, he will not at this point be able to leave until tomorrow in any event because the flights tend to depart in the morning hours. I hope that -- perhaps we will be finished by 11.00. That would be the best thing, obviously. But if we're not, Your Honour, we may ask you to assist us in this way. We do make -- as I'm sure the Chamber knows, we make a considerable effort to try to treat the witnesses as fairly as possible and accommodate them and keep them in The Hague for as short a time as we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you very much for the information you have given us. I simply wish to note, if you allow me, I have some observation with regard to what my learned colleague has just said. I want you to understand that the Defence is very much under pressure. You know all the requirements that we have put, and there is a tremendous burden on us. I want to have a clear conscience vis-a-vis my client and vis-a-vis the job that I am performing. We are doing every -- making every effort to do our job correctly, and we are at the very edge of the efforts we can make. We have been working the whole day, and it is only in the evenings we can write motions and prepare for the cross-examinations, and then we are forced and pressurised to rush things. Your Honours, never in my 25 years of practice that I have found myself in this current situation. Never, wherever I have defended people, and this I have done across the world, never have I found myself in a situation where, due to time, I cannot reflect on justice. So, please, I would ask my learned colleagues that have been preparing this case for five full years, the last testimonies they've taken in March 2001 -- actually, I believe that there is the witnesses' commission. We will accept a schedule be -- of course, the Prosecution is here for a longer period of time than the Defence and they know how business must be conducted. So I kindly ask you, Your Honours, to conclude these proceedings so that the Defence has a clear conscience vis-a-vis their clients, the Court and God. Since I'm pressurised by time, I fear that justice will be -- a detriment will be made to justice. We must need time. These are very serious issues. This is an entire political situation going back ten years we are dealing with. We cannot discuss all this in a month's time. All of us come from different parts of the world, and all of us, we have to learn about culture and political relations and so on and so forth. My client has, before this Court, his last opportunity vis-a-vis himself, his children, and vis-a-vis truth, to come to the material truth, which is something that the Prosecution should be interested in. We are working towards the truth, whatever the truth may be, and for this we need time. Thank you, Your Honours. Secondly, finally we have received notice from the Registry that Mrs. Visnja Drenski Lasan has become legal assistant, so I would like to call upon the Court to allow her to be present in the courtroom, because our colleague, Nika Pinter, will have to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so we will only have Visnja Drenski to help us. That will be all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, let me make sure that I understand what you are saying. That is, you agree that we have another witness at 11.00 this morning, but these kind of things could never happen again in the future. In the future, the Prosecutor will have a much better scheduling of the witness. Is that what you mean? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour, you notice that the Defence has an honourable attitude to all parties here. My client, I would like to add something about him. It is not easy for him in this courtroom. During the past six days, he has suffered tremendously. He didn't want to cry about this, and work has not been interrupted. It is not easy -- the client will, of course, respect the decision. And given the problems that I have noted that I would have with the witness, I have prepared my questions accordingly and I will try to be as brief as possible. But please, in future, take into account what I have just said, because we are really exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This Trial Chamber has taken note of what you said about your client's problem, and we have instructed the registrar to look into this matter in the future. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say also that two very important principles of criminal proceedings, of economy and of justice, are not compatible. But I would like to say that the principle of economics, which is quite understandable to be respected by the Court, and we know that the Court wants to achieve economy and efficiency in the proceedings and have it focussed in the greatest possible manner on the case and on the schedule, because unless you have a schedule in advance, we cannot have an efficient proceedings. And I have been a judge too long not to appreciate this. I truly respect your decisions regardless of the judicial activity and judicial remedies which we will resort to within the frameworks of our code in this country and in the Tribunal. The guidelines that you have given us are truly something to be respected. Now, referring to the economy of judicial proceedings, this does not mean only to be objectivity in pronouncing a sentence, but also a just conduct of proceedings, so not only the burden of proof is with the Prosecution but also with the Defence. We need preparation for cross-examination. If we prepared for cross-examination of Witness U according to a schedule -- we only knew this a day or two in advance, then every disruption of the schedule makes problems for us. So this time, I am saying that I agree with the Prosecution, that we have to be as cooperative as possible, but this causes problems for us. And may I use this opportunity -- I apologise, Your Honours, for intervening. It would be most useful to us, if we are trying to be economical and as brief as possible, we would find it most useful, unless we have longer periods of interruption where we can prepare, but in that case, we would very much like to know the schedule in advance for quite a long time, both in connection with the Court, in connection with breaks, one day, two days, the schedule of calling witnesses. Because I know that the Prosecution has problems calling witnesses because something -- some people just don't want to come, they cannot come on certain dates. And since we have not had any postponement, we understand all this, what we would at least like to know, not only the daily schedule, the weekly schedule and the schedule for several weeks. I hope that you will appreciate this, and the problems that the Defence is having. And thank you for taking up so much of your time, but this will, of course, help us because if we lose half an hour, an hour a day, it can be a gain of one week in our work. If we are briefer and more efficient in the remaining time at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for allowing us to hear the next witness at 11.00. And this Trial Chamber shares your views concerning the time schedule. That's why we announced the time schedule, not only for this week but for next month. And I hope in the future the Prosecutor will provide us another list of witnesses for this month. And as for the legal status of Ms. Lasan, at the moment I have to say that this Trial Chamber has not been informed of that notice from the registrar officially. And as soon as we got those notification, we'll make our decisions accordingly. Thank you. Usher, would you please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, would you please furnish us with a list of the witnesses in accordance with the order for this week and for the week after our court recess, because at least we have to know the updated list for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We will do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, please remember that you are still under the solemn declaration. And this Trial Chamber has granted you the protective measures. Mr. Krsnik. You can continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We will begin our examination today. I have prepared myself so as to have my questions as concise as possible and your answers as brief as possible. I think that we stopped yesterday with the question of the departure of your wife to Belgrade. And my question was: Your wife left by a JNA helicopter to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I believe that I answered the question yesterday. I said that she had departed for Belgrade, but I don't know by which means of conveyance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me: From Mostar, you could leave Mostar by all means of conveyance in those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, because it was -- if you would go by car to Belgrade, you would have many checkpoints, and some of these routes were illegal and only served to take away property from the passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You can go by car or by any other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, you could go by helicopter organised by the Red Cross, in the same way as convoys of buses would go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The helicopters had the insignia of the Red Cross of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I know that helicopters had signs of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said that your wife had told you that the helicopters had the sign, so you talked about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but this does not mean that she flew by helicopter. I don't know why this is so important in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How did you leave Mostar to Belgrade yourself, by what means of conveyance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I went with a freight plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A freight plane of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I expect that the plane was a JNA plane. The pilot was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At that time, not all of the citizens had the same privilege?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course not. I travelled with my boss, and one of his close relatives was the commander at the airport, and he arranged it for us to go and visit our family with the money that we earned working (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I can't remember, believe me. I think I returned to Croatia sometime perhaps in mid-June and back to Mostar by mid-July, sometime around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But then you couldn't see the principal developments in Mostar? I mean the fighting with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I could not; if there was any war, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You don't even know whether there was a war between Croats and Muslims and Serbs or, rather, that the Serbs had committed an aggression against Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, naturally I heard a great deal about it, because my brothers were there and they were engaged in HVO units, and a relative of mine was also in the BH army. I will agree with you when you say that there was an aggression against the JNA by the military and paramilitary JNA formations. But the end of the conflict did not look like a war. It looked more like an understanding, like a pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You were giving very broad answers to my learned friend, that is why I'm asking you, because you said that the absolute power in the defence of Mostar was in the hands of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, well, that is so. That has been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I mean, you were not in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, because there is documents and other evidence. Why should it be important whether I spent in Mostar those two months or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, do you know about the understanding between Izetbegovic and Boban to hand over the conduct of the defence of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I'd be very happy if you could show me that, the document showing that understanding. You know, sir, Krsnik, there were very many agreements that were never respected, because under wartime conditions such agreements remained on paper or, rather, they were never translated into life because one of the two parties defaulted on them, or perhaps both of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, will you please focus on my questions and give me brief questions [as interpreted]. My questions are very simple. Do you know? If you don't [as interpreted] know, then tell us. If you do not know, then also tell us, sir, nothing else. And please refrain from comments, because they do not derive from my questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: And I am answering you like that and, please, I like to be able to answer normally your questions. Your question -- it is impossible to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer questions with a "yes" or "no," and there would be no sense in my coming here to answer your questions with only "yes" or "no" because your questions are very ambiguous so that I cannot answer them in that particular manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware that Izetbegovic and Mate Boban agreed that the defence of Mostar would be entrusted to the HVO in the joint staff headed by Jasmin Jaganjac, a Bosnian or a Muslim, whichever; are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the whole burden of training and armament in that war was borne by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I don't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a party called the "Croat Party of Rights" in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. That was the branch of the Croat Party of Rights from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A branch while Yugoslavia still existed. But after the recognition of Bosnia in 1992 or, rather, the end of this year, the HOS was a party in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: HOS, H-O-S, the Croat defence forces, were the military wing of that party in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, but their chief commander was in Zagreb and the headquarters was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You have personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You were in Zagreb and talked to the supreme commander of those forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I was in Zagreb, but I had no opportunity to talk to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what is the supreme commander called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I do not know how the HOS is structured because I suppose it is structured differently than the BH army, but I think that the head of the Main Staff was Mr. Ante Dzapic and the commander of HOS in Bosnia-Herzegovina was Ante Prkacin, and they are both Croatian nationals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware that the HVO was a part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: As far as I know, the HVO was recognised by the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have not found anywhere, even in the literature, the HVO was recognised by the Presidency, because it is still the Croatian component in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, it is still an organisation apart, even though the war ended eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, my question was: Were they regular, lawful forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you aware of that or not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: My answer is that they were neither regular nor lawful forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know when the Mostar Battalion was formed, do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The Mostar Battalion was formed in April '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that that battalion grew into the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Absolutely, first into the 1st Brigade and then into the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Bozo Rajic, the Defence minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by virtue of a decision of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, issued an order based on the Vance-Owen Plan which the Croats had signed, and the Bosnian or Muslims procrastinated it. But on the basis of the government's decision, an order was issued that in the areas where the Croats constitute the majority, the armed forces would be subordinated to the Croat forces, and in the areas where the Bosniak or Muslim forces were the majority, the Croat forces would be subordinated to the Bosniak Muslim forces, as I said. Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'm aware of that order, but you misinterpreted it completely. The decision of the government was not Bozo -- Bozo Rajic wasn't there. Bozo Rajic took that decision in Mostar or in Grude. The government was in Sarajevo. Bozo Rajic never went to Sarajevo, where we all conducted our consultations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: From the mass media. There are video recordings with those statements, because Bozo Rajic did not attend the session of the government. And I am absolutely positive that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the regular government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would never take a decision which would be directly conducive to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, will you please be so kind as to tell us whether the factories or institutions in Mostar worked at that time in '92? Let's take July, when you came there, until '93, until May '93. Did anything work in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was some work here and there, but mostly to a reduced capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, is that a surprise, that people lost jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course it is not a surprise that people lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Continuing the end of the answer:

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: What comes as a surprise is that only the members of one ethnic group lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, how many refugees -- of course, I'm sure you don't know the number, but perhaps you do. How many Muslim refugees came from Podvelezje and all those neighbouring villages from East Mostar to West Mostar, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, counsel, do not use Muslim refugees. Muslim refugees exist in Pakistan from Afghanistan, so will you please try to use the accepted terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, of course. No problem. What term do you want me to use, "Bosniak"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Sir, well, if you don't know how, I'm really astonished by that fact. Bosniak refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: They are not refugees. They are people who were expelled by the force of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait. Wait. At this moment, I have to remind you both, since you are speaking with the same language, all you have said has to be translated into the other two languages. We entirely rely on the interpreters. So please make a pause after each question and answer so that the interpreters could follow you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: May I ask the Witness and Mr. Krsnik, you're coming very close to the situation that we were in yesterday where you were debating with each other on the basis of your very full knowledge of what happened in the former Yugoslavia, and you are debating as well-informed people rather than trying to assist the Court. I know it's difficult - I said that to you yesterday - but please try to be professional. Your position is to try and elicit information from this witness here which either disparages the evidence that he gave yesterday or puts in issue something that he said yesterday. We haven't yet addressed the issues that came before the Court yesterday. This witness gave very clear evidence of his personal experiences of being a member of an ethnic group, the Muslims or Bosniaks of the former Yugoslavia, who he claims were mistreated during the conflict with the HVO and the other military units that were under that umbrella. You haven't yet addressed that issue. That's what -- this is why this witness is here. What you're doing is very interesting, but it doesn't address the reason why you're cross-examining this witness, unless you take it that there is no dispute at all about what he said yesterday. Isn't that the point of a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But to get to that point, we need to prepare the ground for them and start moving towards them. So now I must speed matters up, and I'm not really sorry that I have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you still owe me an answer to my question. Did those refugees populate West Mostar or didn't they, and how many of them were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: They were not refugees. They were people expelled by the force of arms, and they spread all over the town. Their number, nobody knew it then. Nobody knows it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell us, please, who moved into flats abandoned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: By and large, Croats fled from Central Bosnia, and that remains the case to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember how many statements you gave to the State Security Service in Mostar and the investigators of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I do not remember. I'm not aware that there is a State Security Service in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You do not remember giving a statement to the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I'm still not aware that there's a State Security Service there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the 17th of January, '96?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: '96, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm simply not aware that it exists, or rather that that is its name, the State Security Service of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That is its precise name. Do you remember giving the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I remember giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me -- now, let's move on to the 9th of May. In that statement, you said that you woke up at 4.00 in the morning, and only at 17.45, a quarter to 6.00 in the afternoon, members of the HVO entered your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: That is simply not true. Sir, it must be a mistake in the translation. You say 5.45, and the translator forgot to -- in English, you say it in the same way, 5.45 in the morning and in the afternoon, so the translator simply forgot to put morning rather than afternoon. That is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That is a different matter. You said that it started at 5.00 rather than at 4.00, and they broke into your apartment at 6.00 in the morning. Is that another mistake, or which is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Sir, do you really think that I could remember the exact minute at a time when a town was in flames, when shells were falling all over? I really could not make an accurate assessment to a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, this is what your statement says, which you read and signed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that that was at about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which of them is correct, the first one or the second one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The one that says that I was woken up by the attack in the morning hours, and that they came around 6.00. I really do not know whether this is my first, second, or third statement. You have them before you. I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what is correct? In the first statement you said it was the policemen who came to fetch you. You recognised Braco Poznic. And in your second statement, you said it was Kemal Selmanovic who came to take you away. Now, what is correct, Braco Poznic or Kemal Selmanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: What period of time are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you had enough patience to answer my questions and do not start answering without waiting for the end of my question, then you would be able to hear me. So will you please bear with me and listen to my question to the end.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the events on the 30th of June, 1993, you first stated that you were arrested by two unknown members of the HVO, and that in the street you saw Braco Poznic. In your second statement you said that you were addressed by Kemal Selmanovic, and you mention only him and nobody else. Now, which one of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course, it is true that my flat -- that Mr. Kemal Selmanovic came there and took me out. Braco Poznic was the chief of police, and he was waiting in front of the building. You must have confused certain things in those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, it says very clearly, sir, in your statement that you were arrested by two unknown soldiers, "unknown soldier." You will agree with me that an unknown soldier is an unknown soldier; that is, it is not a known soldier. And secondly, you say in your statements which you signed that you were arrested by Kemal Selmanovic, so this is not the same. Please, if you don't want to answer my question, then you don't have to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I do want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So what is true, that you were arrested by unknown soldiers or by Kemal Selmanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Kemal Selmanovic and an unknown soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In your third statement of the 18th December and the 19th of January this year, that is recently, you said that you stopped working for the BiH army in the summer of 1997. Yesterday in this Court, before this Honourable Court, you said that you stopped working for them after the -- following the Dayton Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: So where is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which one of the two is true? When did you stop working for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Both are true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you always have two truths? Excuse me, Witness. There cannot exist two truths. Did you stop working in '97 or during the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, of course there can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, I should like to remind the counsel not to start speaking until you can see on the transcript the end of the previous sentence -- rather, the previous answer of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I think that question is quite unnecessary. Do you always have two truths? What kind of question is this? You could ask him which is true, but you should not pose any questions like this. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are quite right, Your Honours. But you see, I am exposed to this major pressure. And I assure you, Your Honour, it is very difficult to communicate with this witness. And if you spoke my language, you would understand. Because the witness is trying to dodge my questions. He is evading answers, and I am really at great pain, and I beg of this Chamber to understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this is simply not true. You are asking questions which for the most part have nothing to do with the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's stop the debate between yourselves, but just to bear in mind that you should ask a question in the line of the normal procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will complete my examination with a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the truth? Did you leave the BiH army in 1997, or is it true what you said before this Honourable Court, that you left it during the Dayton Peace Accords? So when did you speak the truth, before this Court or in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: In both cases. If I may, I will explain it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, thank you. There's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think this witness should be allowed to give an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you can see, I am not conducting this examination. It is conducted by Mr. Krsnik. I am only answering his questions. And if the examination follows some other course, then I cannot be held responsible for it. At the time when the Dayton Peace Accords were signed, this document put an end to the belligerences in my homeland of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In view of the kind of work that I did for Bosnia at the time, the need for such work ceased. However, the agency to which I was committed and which brought together people, regardless of the ethnic origin, religion, or membership in an army, was trying to find the missing persons. Unfortunately, the largest number of the missing are on the Bosniak side, a huge number of them. And this is the case to this day. My agency was involved in trying to trace them. So naturally, I remained a soldier, in a way, because the signing of new professional -- agreements were signed with the army. Of course, the army needed people. (redacted), I had no intention -- that is, I did not think that the army would need my services again. So that my contract ended sometime in July '97. And this is my true statement, and I am saying it under full moral and legal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think that you mentioned your profession, so that will have to be removed from the transcript. Is your answer, then, pursuant to Mr. Krsnik's question, is that one part of your work ceased after the Dayton Accord as a military man, but you remained as a civilian in your other work, which was trying to identify where missing people had gone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So if Mr. Krsnik has any questions specifically arising out of that response, which I suppose I elicited rather than you, I mean of course you're free to ask further questions. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and thank you for your help and your understanding. But it is already half past 10.00, and if we wanted to finish with this witness by 11.00, and there is my colleague who has to ask some questions, I really see no purpose in asking any further questions of this witness, because what the Defence wanted to achieve and to show this Honourable Court, I believe we have done this. And with this difficulty in communication, I believe we also saw how difficult it was. But thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start my cross-examination, I would like to ask to resolve a question so as not to have the witness consider me as being provocative or believe that it is an attempt of manipulating with him. In the course of the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Krsnik, there was always the problem of terminology that emerged, whether it was a question of the Bosnian Muslims, Bosniaks, the army of B and H, the Muslim army and the like. This is not only a problem today. It is a problem that we have had with most other witnesses too. I would like, here and now, to resolve this issue with the witness. We also hope that the Chamber will help me in this. The indictment is written in such a way that it speaks exclusively of Bosnian Muslims, by way of terminology. I believe that we must follow the terminology of the indictment. The entire spirit of the indictment reflects the conflict between Muslims and Croats, no armies and so forth. The separation line, which is a problem in our case, which you can see from the indictment and which can be seen from the situation on the ground, is a conflict. On the one side, we had the Muslims, and on the other side, the Croats. We cannot obliterate things here. We cannot discuss how we shall call one another, whether they were at the time a TO, or army of B and H, or Muslim forces, as it is stated in the indictment. I would like to have this problem resolved so as to avoid further problems and to have discussions with the witness on this and to say that we are perhaps provoking and manipulating with things that are below the level of the work we are doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you that we should follow the terms that appear in the indictment, in principle. But as for the particular witness if there is two terms which express the same meaning and one of which is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not so sensitive to that witness, with the understanding that the two terms expresses a meaning, you could use that one. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear to me, and I will abide by your instructions. Could you tell the Prosecutor to acquaint the witness with the terms used in the indictment and that the Defence, by using other terms, has no intention of provoking the witness? And now I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, can I say something? We are dealing with a very sensitive situation, and we recognise that all of you come from different sides and you have sensitivities too, as well as the witnesses. I think that the ordinary rules of courtesy must apply, and I'm sure that having practised at the Bar - and I believe that Mr. Seric was a judge - that you know how to deal courteously with people. It is normal to ascertain in advance what term they find acceptable. Now, I think you know, from listening - and I think we're beginning to know, from listening to witnesses - that there are certain terms which were used yesterday afternoon in the space of a very short time that are utterly, utterly unacceptable to any of the parties, whether you come from the Serb side, the Croat side or the Bosniak Muslim side. They are certain terms that we've heard expressed, and unfortunately they were being used yesterday, I thought quite unnecessarily, but that's a personal view. If we can avoid using those three pejorative terms. And if you ascertain, I think, with your normal education, you will see what terms were used yesterday which caused pain and try to avoid them today. And I'm sure the witness is listening to what we're saying, and he appreciates the difficulties from the Bench and from both sides, and that he will cooperate as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was such kind of proposal from the Defence counsel that we should get our witness acquainted with the indictment. It seems to me that this question, this proposal, it is misleading. I think that the indictment is written in a succinct language and there is a line between HVO and AbiH as participants in the military conflict. I suggest that my learned colleague should read the indictment before raising this question here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to say that the disagreement did not come from the words "Bosnian Muslim" but "Muslim refugees." The witness said that these were people who had been expelled by the force of arms and did not leave voluntarily. So the difficulty is not at the level "Bosniak Muslim" but the attributes added to this to further explain their particular condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understood this. I do not wish to continue the discussion on this. I understood your instructions. I hope that I've been understood that my intention was a good one, just to avoid misunderstandings. And as far as what Judge Clark has said, that we could clear up what is offensive to the witness, well, we can do this now. Well, I would like to say that we have never been or will be offensive to the witness. So may I begin my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, through the discussion, I suppose that you have understood what is controversial, and so we should perhaps decide on the terms that you find offensive. Do you wish, instead of using the word "Muslims," use the term "Bosniaks"; is that what you wish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Counsel, as you know, that I have always used the term "Croatian army" or "HVO." Imagine if I were to ask you, "What term would you like, 'Croatian army,' 'Ustasha army,' or 'Catholic army'?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose I had -- ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You should not announce any words of offence to Defence counsel. That's not a good practice, I have to warn you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had no intention of doing this. I just wanted to say how different the terms are. There are Muslims in Afghanistan, in Pakistan and elsewhere. The legal term is "Bosniak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, why don't you begin your questions, and when we come across this issue, we will try to solve it with some alternative terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: With the leave of the President, could we try, unless it's material to an issue, to avoid the use of those which we -- I don't understand what they mean, but I gather that they are very pejorative terms, and one is "Ustasha," the other one is "Chetnik," and the third one is "balija." None of us know what they mean, but we know that everybody is deeply offended. So could we, unless the use of the word -- you disagree with me, Mr. Krsnik. You're not offended?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see, so that we've got it wrong. But it seems to cause electric impulses in this court if those words are used, so could we avoid them and we agree to avoid them? And that rule applies to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree. May we begin, finally?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My name is Zelimir Par, and I'm one of the counsel for Vinko Martinovic. Yesterday you spoke of an event taking place in 1992, when allegedly a soldier from the Vinko Martinovic unit killed a person with impunity, and you cited this as an example of the privileged position of the Vinko Martinovic unit. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Well, in connection with that testimony, I would like to ask you whether you are aware of when that ATG Mrmak or Vinko Skrobo was formed. Do you know that it was formed only in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So we agree that it was formed in 1993 and that the event you cited was from 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, Vinko Martinovic had his unit in 1992, but it was not called that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No, we are discussing the ATG, Vinko Martinovic and Skrobo, and I asked you specifically for that unit. Now I would like to discuss the event. Will you tell us, once again, what was the name of the person who was killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I think his name was "Dragan Bojcic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the killing took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: In a cafe in the centre of the city. I don't know the name. It was eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When did the killing exactly take place; can you tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I cannot remember the date. I was not an eyewitness to the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me -- can you tell me the name of the person who did the killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. The name was "Azer Kajan."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Have you personally checked in the court, police, whether anything has been done about the case, whether the case has been recorded, whether charges had been brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I have no legal foundations for doing that, but I heard personally from him. He simply boasted about it, and nothing was -- no charges were brought against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So your knowledge is based on his stories and the knowledge of other people. Since you have said that this had happened, you testified before this Court that this had happened, now you, as a person with some intelligence and experience, how would you assess the quality of that information that you have stated to the Court? And the information that you have described here, would you describe as being verified, reliable information or simply a story and a rumour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I would say that this was a very bad piece of information. It was necessary just to say, in that connection, that some people from the unit had privileges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So we have cleared up the quality of that information. Secondly, something that you testified about yesterday and which dates back 20 years, and that is the juvenile delinquency of Vinko Martinovic. And in order to discredit him, you spoke of the fact that he had been in fact sentenced as a juvenile. Do you personally know what this was about, what kind of verdict it was, for what was he held responsible; have you any personal knowledge about that particular situation or did you simply hear about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course I heard about it, because we lived in the same part of the town. I'm not a judge, this was not accessible to me, and I have no intention of discrediting Mr. Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that after a certain period of time following verdict, that the verdict is simply wiped away, and especially in the case of minors; do you know that such a provision exists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, I'm not competent in the matter, but if I were asked, I would delete that verdict and the sentence straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Have you ever been sentenced yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we go into a private session now, because I would like to discuss an event where the names of potential witnesses may be mentioned and other things that might identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. Before we start with the next witness, we'd like to express our gratitude not only to the Trial Chamber but also to the Defence for the flexibility that they've shown this morning in allowing us to take this next witness out of turn. I think I can say that they can expect to find the same degree of flexibility from our side when it comes time for the Defence to call their witnesses. Mr. President, this witness has requested protective measures, that of a pseudonym and the use of facial distortion. I can inform the Trial Chamber that although this witness does not reside in the territory of the former Yugoslavia any more, she does reside in another part of Europe and has informed me that she is very anxious to have these protective measures granted for her protection and primarily for the protection of her child. And that is her position, and I informed her that I would convey that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there is no objections from Defence counsel. Thank you, thank you very much. So the protective measures are granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Then I believe we can bring the witness into the courtroom. In the meantime, I can inform the Trial Chamber that this witness will testify in respect of paragraphs 7, 18 and 19 of the indictment, which relate to the involvement of the Republic of Croatia in respect of international armed conflict, and also paragraphs 15 and 24, relating to superior authority of the accused Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for this witness is "V" as in "Victor," and it's Exhibit Number PW22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: In English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't matter which way. [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a sheet of paper which we're prepared to give the witness, and I would ask the usher to give that to her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, could I ask you to just simply look at that paper and, without saying anything, tell us whether the information that is contained on that sheet of paper is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, all the information is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, let me ask you, on the sheet of paper that you've just looked at, does that accurately indicate what was your occupation in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Witness V, let me ask you, were you present in the city of Mostar on the 10th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if you recall, what was that day? Did it have any special significance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It was Easter day, and it was also the day when, during the Second World War, the Nazi puppet state of independent State of Croatia was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What did you do on that day? A (redacted) I got invitation to attend Easter celebration in small banquet room of Hotel Ero in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, it's not necessary for you to state out loud your occupation, and I'll ask that that be redacted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You indicated that you were invited to attend an Easter celebration in a hotel. Again for the record, what was the name of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It was Hotel Ero. I'll spell it for you. It's E-R-O.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where is the hotel located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It's located near Santici Street, near Carinski Bridge in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and the witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, did you, in fact, attend the banquet on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was present in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How many people attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: From 20ish, 30ish, between those two figures. I didn't count them in my head, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you say it was a large or a small group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It was smallish group, not that large. It was small banquet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you recall the names of some of the people who were present when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: When I arrived, there were clerical bishop of Catholic church. There was Bishop Paridge. Then there was Franciscan clergy in there. There was Jadranko Prlic, which was at the time prime minister of Herceg-Bosna, president of HVO Herceg-Bosna. He was cohost of the banquet together with Jadran Topic. He was mayor of Mostar at that time. There was then Bruno Stojic. Then there were some other people. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the witness very quickly -- and I know she speaks English, so it rolls off her tongue -- has mentioned a number of names that are not showing up on my monitor in any fashion, except for one. I think that should be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, you and the Prosecutor are speaking the same language, so my advice is that you should pause after he asks the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'll do that from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And in front of you, there is a monitor. And every word you say will be typed out on that screen. If you see, you know, the sentence finished, you could begin to answer the question. And yes, indeed, there are some words, some names, missing in the transcript. Would you please clear it up, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I'll just take you back to the names that you've mentioned. First of all, you mentioned the name of Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you please spell that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: She typed it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just spell it for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: P-r-l-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Jadran --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Jadran Topic. T-o-p-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: S-t-o-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who was Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Bruno Stojic was Minister of Interior for Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you could just briefly describe for us what was taking place at this banquet when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: When I arrived, it was meant to be an Easter banquet, so people were just having a glass of champagne and wine and some food. The normal -- what a banquet would look like normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Subsequently, did any other people arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: We were standing there and chatting. And suddenly, the doors opened. It's a double door, so it opened that way. And Gojko Susak, which is S-u-s-a-k, arrived, followed by Mate Boban, B-o-b-a-n, and then they were accompanied by Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, the guy accused in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple questions about that. Who was Gojko Susak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Gojko Susak was Minister of Defence of Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: He was dressed in the civilian clothing, in a suit. I think it was a dark navy suit -- sorry, dark grey suit. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who was Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Mate Boban was president of HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the president of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It's Croatian Democratic Union, Croatian Nationalistic Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said also that they were accompanied by Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: He was -- he had civilian t-shirt and uniform over it, just like a pullover without the sleeves. And pants were also part of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It was the standard issue HVO uniform, which was those with mask with different colours, those masked uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What colour was the uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It was green, brownish mixture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Camouflage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Camouflage, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after these three persons arrived, what took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I just repeat how they arrived. They came into the room with raised right hand in the Nazi salute, saying "bog i hrvati" for homeland ready. That was their entrance. They shook hands with a few people and started talking to -- predominantly talking to -- actually, a whole group of the people that were inside just encircled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you hear the conversation that took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, I heard conversation clearly, because the banquet room was half size of this courtroom, so we were all very near to each other so we could hear each other clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, again just for the record, perhaps you could spell for us the Croatian words that you just mentioned about "homeland ready."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: "Dom", "D" for "David", "O", "M" for "Mother" -- sorry, can we do it again? Z-A. The next word is D-O-M. The next word is "S" for "Sugar", "P" for "Peter", R-E, "M" for "Mother", "N" for "Nothing", "I".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you forgot to make the break that the President has asked you to make after every question. Will you please take care.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Witness V, I want to ask you to tell us, if you recall, what was said during this banquet by Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I had the impression Mr. Susak was very much in charge. So he started talking to Jadranko Prlic and asking whether they were ready. He started mentioning some account. He asked whether there was sufficient funds in that account. I can only suspect which account can that be. But he told him -- but Susak told him that if he needed money, he will be ready to supply it. Then he asked -- then he started talking to them, saying to them that they are weak, that there is still some Muslim soldiers in their forces. Then they were interrupted by Mr. Naletilic, who said -- who started bragging, basically, how good job his guys have done in Gornji Vakuf, which was also one of the places that took some fighting before that. Susak then went on, saying how they gonna drive Muslims out of the city, how they gonna create pure ethnic -- pure Mostar. And then he was interrupted and asked whether -- because in the same time as banquet was going on, in the separate room there was a president of HDZ for Mostar and president of -- Mr. Stojan Vrljic. I'll spell it. V-R-L-J-I-C is his surname. And also Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, H-A-D-Z-O-S-M-N-O-V-I-C [sic]. He was president of the SDA for Mostar rather than SDA for all of Herzegovina. They had some talks where they apparently meant to settle the differences between the two parties and to find some peaceful solution. After being reminded of that, Susak just said, "No, nothing will come out of it. We'll do our job regardless of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Witness V, you mentioned there a reference to "Muslims in their forces." What forces are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I was referring to HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you hear Susak or Boban -- well, let me ask you, first of all, did you hear other references to Muslims and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: They were referring to Muslims as some strange, awkward name of "balija," which I myself don't know the proper meaning. That's something to offend them. And it was Susak mainly who called them, and as well as General Tuta. That's how he was also -- he was referred during the conversation as "General Tuta."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned the names of a number of people whom you saw at this banquet. Did there appear to be any sort of hierarchy among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Susak was definitely in charge. Boban just stood aside. He hardly uttered a few sentences. And then there was some -- as I thought, someone responsible for the military operation, and that was General Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, later that day -- let me ask you: How long, then, did you stay at this banquet? How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Maybe an hour and a half. Not that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then after the banquet, did you see any reports of this banquet in the media on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I heard first of all Susak saying how they gonna meet at 1900 hours at his place in Siroki Brijeg. I came home that evening and I basically told to my mother what I heard. We were watching the news, and one of the features was the banquet where all of us -- because we were warned not to record, all of us, when they entered, and I saw the people who were on banquet prior to three of them coming inside the room. They showed just that part of banquet on HTV, which is a Croatian television, on the evening news, 10.30 news. After that, they showed some report of Susak meeting some UN officials in Zagreb as if he was in Zagreb, as if he didn't come to Herzegovina at all. It just basically trying to cover it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, if you can, can you look around the courtroom and tell us if you see anyone here who was present at the banquet on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It's the second person from the right in the back row.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And who is that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: That's General Tuta, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the record indicate that the witness has identified the accused Naletilic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examinations. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness V.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And how are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I'm fine, thank you. Very well, thank you, actually. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May I ask that the usher please put the ELMO down so I can see this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Carry on in Croatian if it's easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me what month and year that you left Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I had a Croatian passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me when you received the Croatian passport?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me, please, what the circumstances of your moving

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, this witness is under some protective measures. We'd better not go into the details about the identity of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you need, we could just go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe that the witness had indicated on her own where she lived, so I didn't believe that that would have been anything that would have been protected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not indicate. You asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, if you want to continue, we'll go into private session. I think that's the very easy way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We don't need to do that right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness V, was it very easy for you to obtain this Croatian passport in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, because Franjo Tudjman was giving it to every Croat that was born and lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I myself am half-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you have -- excuse me. When you moved to the country in which you now live, did you continue with your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, we come to this question again. I've already said that if you need to ask those questions, we could easily go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You testified that it was an occasion where people were drinking and eating. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And everybody was having a good time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, chatting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me what sort of drinks were available at this gathering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: There was some champagne, some wine, some soft drinks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Was there also beer and hard liquor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Probably it was, but I wasn't looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you notice other people among the guests who were drinking beer or hard liquor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I can't recall those particular details. I never look what people are drinking, I'm sorry, only what I choose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In the witness statement that you gave the Office of the Prosecutor, you were interviewed by one interviewer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me how that interview came about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I called, myself, Tribunal after knowing that these two witnesses -- these two accused are going to have trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So then would it be a fair statement to say that you learned through some media sources that Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic had been indicted by this Tribunal, so you came and volunteered your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you volunteered your testimony to the Office of the Prosecutor for any other accused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I'm waiting for one more to be accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So when you had -- did they come to your country to interview you, or did they bring you here or elsewhere to interview you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: They came to my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And the interview took place on two separate days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was a very comprehensive interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it that comprehensive because we had normal conversation, which gentleman noted, and then he came next day and -- actually, I read the statement with him standing next to me, and I just basically signed it. Made a few corrections, names and things like that which were misspelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: During this interview process, it was very clear that the Office of the Prosecutor was targeting Mr. Naletilic. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Wasn't it clear to you that you were there to give testimony against Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I wanted to give testimony against Mr. Naletilic. I did it of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you gave a full and truthful account to the Office of the Prosecutor on these two days, in February of 2001 and March 1st of 2001, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I gave them truthful version of all events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review the statement which you gave prior to your testimony today?
