utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I read it over two days ago, just briefly, not even all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you never once indicated that Mr. Naletilic made any sort of gestures concerning the homeland ready, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I mentioned that. I'm very much aware of that, because being the person as I am, I always opposed any kind of fascist behaviour, and that stuck in my mind for eight and-a-half years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While it may have been stuck in your mind for eight and-a-half years, can you tell this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, why it wasn't in your extensive nine-page statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I think it was originally, but since it's very hard to translate it in English, they just probably omitted based on that reason. Because if I told you now, "za dom spremni, bog i hrvati," would you be able to jot it down immediately? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May the Trial Chamber, please, advise this witness that she is to answer questions and not ask questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you hear Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At the time of this Easter party at the Hotel Ero in Mostar, you did not personally know Mr. Naletilic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, I did not. I never mixed with people of such milieu.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You had no knowledge of his background or history, had you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, I heard bits and pieces, but generally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned that there was the, for example, head of the Franciscan church in Mostar was at this Easter party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That the mayor of Mostar was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That the head of the Franciscan church for Herzegovina was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And there were many reporters present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You indicate that Mr. Susak was, in your opinion, in charge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that is the feeling that you got. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: That's the impression I had after what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You -- would it be a fair statement, Witness, that you did not agree with these statements made by Mr. Susak and Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, I did not agree ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you speak up that day and tell Mr. Susak and Mr. Boban that you did not agree with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: With all the fire-power that they had in their hands, and criminal backgrounds, no, I did not dare to say anything then and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would it be a fair statement that the head of the Franciscan church for Mostar and the other head of the Franciscan church for Herzegovina, they also did not disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: They did not disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Nobody made speeches at this gathering, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No. It was more informal gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And with 30 -- approximately 30 people there speaking for a 10- or 15-minute period, how could you hear the conversation between Susak, for example, or Boban, for example, or Mr. Naletilic, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: When Susak spoke, everybody listened. They didn't argue back. So he had that tone of voice, so I could hear his word, the accused word quite correctly, because it's a small room. People standing in a circle. So these people could just stand into a circle, a half circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In the meantime, if I understand your testimony, the party is still going on and people are still talking with each other and mingling. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, party turned in a completely different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Naletilic was born and raised in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Probably. I maybe have heard, but didn't matter to me because I never had any contact whatsoever with people of lower class than I was, if I may say in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So are you saying that Mr. Naletilic is a lower-class person than you, Ms. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that, and I respect each and every human being as they are. But being from upper middle-class family, I didn't have any sort of conversation which I would hold with somebody who is -- who has probably only primary school. We didn't have the chance to mix.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you didn't -- you don't realise, then, and did not realise, that Mr. Naletilic left Bosnia-Herzegovina when he was 18 years old and sought asylum in Germany from the communists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It didn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You were not aware, then, were you, that Mr. Susak was also born in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I really don't see the relevant point in that. What's so special about Siroki Brijeg? I had friends from there, and they are all fine people. Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness V, the relevance of anything is going to be determined by these three Judges.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Apologise to Judge. I just couldn't contain myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were not aware, then, that Mr. Susak and Mr. Naletilic were childhood friends. You were not aware that Mr. Naletilic had lived in Germany or outside of the Bosnia-Herzegovina area until approximately 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I heard some bits and pieces, that he was somewhere abroad. I didn't know that he was in Germany, what he was doing there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You were not then aware that after he had moved and sought asylum in Germany at a young age, that he became a businessman and owned restaurants and casinos; you were not, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Not even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me whether or not you have any background in military organisations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So if I were to ask you if it is a military jargon to call soldiers "boys," you wouldn't know, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I would know that because that is part of the common knowledge which educated people do know. I wouldn't go into too many details of the military operations - that's something for the experts - but the common stuff from the military, yes, I would know because I would have read it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Being that Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Susak were childhood friends, and also given the fact that you've testified that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- were not comfortable in speaking up and saying anything to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, I saw Mr. Stringer standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I object. The witness doesn't know if Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Susak were childhood friends. I don't think there's any evidence in the record on that point at all, other than the fact that that has been repeated numerous times by various counsel for Mr. Naletilic. So I would object to putting questions to the witness based on matters which are beyond the personal experience and knowledge of the witness and which are also not part of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, the witness has already said that she didn't know that Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Susak were childhood friends as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know where that objection comes from, but I also must say that that's one of the problems in the proceeding in this Trial Chamber and in this Tribunal. We will prove this in our case, but we cannot bring this witness back because of the problems with travel distances. So I will try to rephrase my questions so it will be not objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if Mr. Meek is proposing to make this witness his witness for purposes of his case in chief, we don't object. We agree that the witness should not be brought back again and inconvenienced for that purpose. So I wouldn't have an objection to that. We would, however -- I think that does then change the manner in which Mr. Meek puts his questions to the witness, if in fact she's now testifying in the nature of a direct examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, you may rephrase your question and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I'm not turning this witness into my witness. I just want to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness V, assuming that Susak and Mladen Naletilic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Meek. I think the correct way to do it is, "My client will call evidence to this effect," and then put to the witness what your case is and is going to be so it's on the record and she has an opportunity to make her observations on what your case is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness V, my client will call evidence to the effect that he and Mr. Susak were childhood friends from Siroki Brijeg from a very young age and remained friends through 1991. Is it so hard for you to imagine that a childhood friend of Mr. Susak, such as Mladen Naletilic, would also be fearful to disagree with Mr. Susak, especially in a meeting such as the one you described, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic supported Susak's argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness V, didn't you also support that argument by omission, by not speaking up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, I never supported. I was just scared to confront him then and there. If I had a bomb, maybe I would blow myself apart, but I didn't have any weapons because I never carried weapons. If I had the weapons, they would be dead, then and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you feel such hatred against Mr. Naletilic that you would have killed him then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I do not feel hatred towards anybody, including both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The point is I could never agree with the fascist language, with the actions that they were clearly planning. I could never agree with that against any ethnic, national, whatever group, Martians, doesn't matter. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness V. Fortunately, you and I both speak English, and I'm reading the transcript and you said that if you would have had a weapon, they would have been dead. Is that not a fact, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you feel the same way today, I take it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: If you were to do the same thing and planned to exterminate whoever, I would be against you, yes. And I never met you before, as I never met them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Witness V, you do not have any evidence for this Trial Chamber that my client in fact planned to exterminate anybody, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: If they were gonna evict Muslims, if they gonna swim across Neretva, as they were saying, if Mostar is gonna be pure Croatian city, then it means that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Witness V, these things that you just said now, you did not say in your statement that you gave to the OTP, nor did you testify in your direct examination, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I did, and you should have read the statement. And I said that they gonna expel the Muslims. I said that in the statement and I said in the direct examination by Mr. Doug.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness V, you never indicated in any statement or in any examination under oath today that Mr. Naletilic or Mr. Susak intended to exterminate anybody, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I think "extermination" also implies expelling people, people swimming across the rivers, making pure Croatian city. How you gonna make it? By eliminating people, and that's extermination. So Muslims wouldn't be present in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, you would agree that there are different ways that a person can support another person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I agree, but this was clearly because -- was Mate Boban that childhood friend? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No. Listen to the question, Witness, please. Would you agree that a person can be supported by another person in various ways?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: -- Mr. Naletilic clearly stated his guys have done job in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: You were scared to speak up, your fellow colleagues were scared to speak up, the other people who you've described that were at this function were scared to speak up; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Why is it so unusual --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Why is it, ma'am, so unreasonable that Mr. Naletilic, being a childhood friend or crony of Mr. Susak, would also have been scared to speak up, and scared to go against anything that he would say in public, and in fact might even go along with something so he would not be injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic at that time had his Convicts' Battalion, and I didn't have single gun. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Witness V, what proof do you have today about the comment you just made, that Mr. Naletilic had the Convicts' Battalion? What proof do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I recall when I first saw Mr. Naletilic, I can pinpoint in Western Herzegovina where his headquarters were. I know that his men, which I met -- I was meeting every day -- I worked in that particular company where I had access to people. I saw him at that headquarter. They were all swearing to him, always talking about that general. He had some probably very -- very big influence on very young guys who were in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can we get a date on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: On this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Which date are we speaking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Prior to that, you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would this be --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Because I worked down there and I had daily meetings with various numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So what you're saying, if I understand you correctly, is that you base this on what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, but from very reliable sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Exactly. And your testimony under oath has been that prior to the Easter celebration in Mostar, you had only seen Mr. Naletilic one time in Siroki Brijeg --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I mentioned. On the way to Siroki Brijeg, there was his headquarter, and I saw him in front of his headquarter. That's the only time I saw him prior to the event. I talked to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Diarra, please. Microphone for Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't need the microphone. This was just an exchange. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise, but I did not catch the exchange between the Judge and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's all right. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you indicated in your direct examination that you received an invitation to this function, was that in writing, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I received the invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you have a copy of that with you or did you keep one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I don't have any of my property down there, so, no, I don't have that invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the invitation didn't mention anybody specifically who would be there, did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, it didn't mention anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you're familiar with TV journalism, I take it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you're aware of foul footage, the term "foul footage"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So on the evening in question, after you had left this function and were with your mother, watching TV, it could have very well been that the clip you observed of Mr. Susak was nothing but foul footage; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it was, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question to clarify. The Bishop of Mostar was actually at this party; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Ratko Peric. "P" for "Peter", "E", "R" for "Romeo", "I" for "India", "C" for "Charlie".

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric, do you have any questions in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness, in her testimony, did not mention the client, and therefore we have no reason -- we have no ground for any cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's just one issue, Mr. President. I'll gladly take any guidance from the Trial Chamber on how I ought to proceed. The witness, in her cross-examination from Mr. Meek, the words "extermination" and "expel" came up, particularly in terms of what she said or didn't say in the witness statement. Counsel did not put the witness statement to the witness, so that she didn't have an opportunity to see what she did or didn't say on that issue during her interview with the investigator. However, in my view, I think counsel did attempt to impeach the witness to some extent by trying to draw a distinction or difference between what she said today and what she said previously. And so with the Trial Chamber's permission or guidance, I would like to -- I would ask to have an opportunity to rehabilitate on this issue - we call it back home "prior consistent statements" - which is something that can be done with leave of the Trial Chamber if a witness has been shown or if there's been a suggestion of a prior inconsistent statement during the cross-examination. What I would like to ask the Trial Chamber, if I could simply put the witness statement to the witness so that she could state exactly what she said on that issue during the interview that she was asked about during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Meek is standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I believe that I did exactly ask this witness if she had reviewed her statement given to the OTP, and she said yes, she had reviewed her statement that was given to the OTP prior to her testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said not completely, and you can read it over. I apologise to Judge, but I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This has been a continuing, ongoing problem with the witness prior to this, and that problem is the witnesses seem to jump into questions when we try to speak to the Judges. I think it's highly inappropriate, and I wish that they could be directed not to do so. But I would just say, Your Honours, that she was asked whether she read the statement that she prepared, she indicated she had reviewed that prior to her testimony, and now I think it's inappropriate to now let her review it again. It's not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecutor has the right to show the witness the statement and to refresh her recollections on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to lay a foundation for doing that before proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, you were asked during your cross-examination about the interview you gave to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you recall that interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you referred to a statement which you then signed after that interview was completed, which is dated the 26th of February and the 1st of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: -- switch the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In that interview, or in that statement, I should say, do you recall what, if anything, you said about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you're going about this in a very laboured way. She made a statement. She admitted she made a statement. There's no dispute that she made a statement. Bring her straight to the point that's in conflict. You're entitled to do this. You don't have to lay the ground. You're not impugning the witness. You're confusing, in my view, the procedure for declaring a witness hostile. This is your own witness. An issue has arisen. Take her straight to the point. We know that she has made a statement. We don't have to waste time on that. Just take her straight to the statement and then furnish us with the part of the statement that you want to draw her attention to. We know what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. I will then do that. I will ask the usher if the usher can provide a copy of this document to the witness. I'm going to refer the witness to the bottom last appearing on page 7. I have -- the Trial Chamber, I think, declined to look at the statement -- there was a previous time we refreshed recollection. I think the Trial Chamber declined to look at the statement at that time. I have an additional copy, actually an additional number of copies, which I could provide if the Trial Chamber would like to see those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps, first of all, you establish that she did say something; and then if she does agree that she said it and you find it, then maybe we will have a look at it. If you don't, if you don't establish that it was said, maybe we won't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness V, if I could direct your attention to the last paragraph on page 7, and if you could read that paragraph to yourself, I'm then going to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yeah, I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Does that paragraph refresh your memory as to whether you said anything about any intentions in respect of the Muslims in Mostar, whether anything was said at this banquet on that issue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It says clearly that they talked in general terms of getting rid of the Muslims, and that was the talk that they had. It was a common talk among Croatian nationalists at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall informing the investigator of that during the course of this interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I told him that. I told him the words, but I didn't think that mattered that much. I summed it up, getting rid of Muslims, general talk of getting rid of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We have a problem here, Mr. Stringer, of coming from different jurisdictions. But the general principle that is common to all our legal systems is that we are in search of justice. Now, the normal way when the contents of a statement are disputed - and it's the Prosecution case that certain words were said and it's the Defence case that words were not said - it is normal for you to identify a passage and to establish that the Prosecution's position is correct or, indeed, it could be the Defence position is correct, if it's a Defence witness. But all we've had is some generalities. You brought this witness back and brought the statement back to assist the Court. And as far as I understand you, your position is that this witness did, indeed, say words that the Defence deny she used. Now, you haven't brought us, or this witness, to the words or the paragraphs. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the witness is referring to the bottom -- the last paragraph appearing on page 7 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If you look at the transcript, you asked, Do you recall informing the investigator -- no, it says clearly that they talked in general terms of getting rid of the Muslims, and that was the talk that they had. Is that a synopsis by this witness of what she said, or is it actually what she said? That isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, having looked at that part of your witness statement, can you tell us, if you can, what exactly are the words that you used in describing this issue as contained in your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: They said repeatedly they will expel Muslims from Mostar, Muslims will swim across the River Neretva, which is the river dividing the city. And they are going to make Mostar Croatian, pure Croatian city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, when you make reference to those statements, how is that referred to in the witness statement which is in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I told Terry these things, and I just summed it up, saying they were basically referring they were going to get rid of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the witness statement, you said, "They talked in general terms of getting rid of the Muslims." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Unless I have failed to clarify this to the Trial Chamber's satisfaction, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to do the cross-examination again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, it would be re-cross-examination, Your Honour. He had several questions, and I only have then a couple more questions I need to ask. Slow it down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there should be an end of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There must be an end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- of the cross-examination, there should be an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I will bring it to an end very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it very important to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So as an exception, I will allow you to do that, but your cross-examination is subject to re-examination, or re-re-examination, you have to bear in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness V, when you gave your witness statement on the two days, you spoke in English, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We all understand that the witness is not a lawyer. She could not distinguish the terminologies we use in the indictment or in the daily life, so when the Chamber evaluates this evidence, we will take note of that. And I will ask the Prosecutor to furnish us with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We will do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Diarra has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you were sent this invitation, did the inter-ethnic tension - I have to speak about that, I'm sorry - but was it already noticeable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was obvious, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were invited personally or representing the profession? Will you please tell me who was it that invited you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I really don't know because we were getting too many invitations at a certain point. But I know that I was asked (redacted) to go in there. It was most probably addressed to me. And to this day, I really can't understand why did he do that. Because he knew my stance, he knew that I could never, ever agree. And I was probably only not pure Croat in that room. I was the only non-pure Croat in that room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was it an invitation to the festivity, and you were not going there to express your views on ethnic groups or to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- receive something from Tuta or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: -- celebration, but it turned out into something else. Yes, I was, in previous, to many Easter, Christmas celebration. I don't have any objections against that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for giving the evidence. We wish you good luck.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When the blinds are pulled down, the usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stringer, what do you suggest us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears that there is a pretty short period of time between now and the lunch break. The Prosecutor will propose to break now for lunch, and then to continue after lunch with the continued cross-examination of Witness U.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please give us a rough idea who will be the next witness, I mean, after this afternoon's witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I can do so in private session, Mr. President, because I think the next witness is asking for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, please continue with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would kindly ask to have a private session, because we are dealing with a set of questions for which we need protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, you were still at the Heliodrom. And I would like to ask you something to do with the Croat units that you mentioned, that you said were at the Heliodrom. If you remember, you mentioned yesterday that allegedly, there was a Croatian unit, a unit from Croatia, from Osijek. And you told us roughly about its technical and operative tasks in Mostar. Is that correct, and do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because we could watch them from the second floor of the school that we were kept in.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. And that is where I'm heading. Looking through this window, could you really learn all about their technical tasks in Mostar? How could you learn all that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, of course I could not, just by looking through the window. The HVO soldiers who were in the barracks -- at first we could see from the window which part of the city was being shelled because it was all aflame. And an hour or two later, HVO soldiers started hugging one another, congratulating -- and congratulating somebody, I presume the unit of that Croatian -- unit from Croatia, that is, and I overheard a discussion. I heard them say, "We'll be at Blagaj in no time."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Tell us -- later on during your investigations and in your analysis later on, you could gather different information. Did you ask for and did you get information about what you have just told us? Did you ever try to relate the later knowledge that you acquired with what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No. It wasn't all that interesting. It happened only one day, and I spent two months working with regard to some other Croatian units. What I learned was that some 50 men from that unit from Croatia were killed in the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I'm trying to make a distinction between your direct knowledge and what you learned at a later date. You spoke about numerous prisoners killed at the front line, about their woundings and so on and so forth. And so my question is as follows: Did -- that knowledge is the result of your subsequent investigations,

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: (redacted) or is it something that you learned directly personally in the camp? Could you tell apart, and can we then try to differentiate between what you know personally and what you heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to warn you that this witness is under the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I really tried not to specify the job or the post. I tried somehow to put it in general terms, and I hope I did not imperil this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, sorry. I'm having a terrible difficulty following the translation, and the translator seems under pressure as well. You speak fast, that's your style, and I think she can keep up with that. Where we're having a problem is that as soon as your question is finished, the witness replies. So could both of you give us, who don't understand your language, a chance. I mean, it's a question of both of you are doing it. We have it whenever witnesses are speaking the same language as the interrogator. So could you just try to remember, because it's impossible for us to make sense of this very important evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If you are ready to answer this, will you please do that and draw the distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Well, my question has to do with differentiating between the information that you presented during your evidence. I'm referring to prisoners, victims and so on. So my question is: How can we differentiate between your personal -- between what you personally saw and what you learnt at a later stage? Could you tell us, how can we then say -- tell which is which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely. Anything that I say here is based exclusively on what I saw and experienced in a camp. Whenever I mention something that I heard from others, I will say so.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were you ever put in what is usually termed as a "human shield"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No. I told you that I was prohibited from leaving the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever personally see a prisoner of war being wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, but I saw very many wounded in my room.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now I should like to ask you to look at a map, because I want to discuss the positions of the Vinko Skrobo unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can the usher please help me? This is Exhibit 14.5, and Prosecution's exhibit. And now I would like to show you this photograph and will ask you to focus, because I have some questions to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could this photograph be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, if you could do this.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness U, can you find your way about this? Are you familiar with this part of the town and do you know what this photograph represents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I recognise it very well indeed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you now use the pointer - you will find it in front of you - and will you please show where was Vinko Skrobo ATG or Mrmak positioned? Can you please show it to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: This is the photograph of Mostar after the war, not before the war. This is the renewed Health Centre. South of it, here, is the Franciscan convent. To the north is the secondary school and the Spanish Square. I think that Mr. Martinovic's unit operated in this area, precisely in the area shown on this photograph. That is what I think. I had no opportunity during the war to see that because I never left the camp during the war, so I had no opportunity to see that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, will you please take one of the markers and make -- and circle what you believe was the zone that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I think it's this part from the Health Centre to the south, so so-called "Gospin Park" which is next to the church.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Will you please just make a circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Well, there is not really any need to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, just a few minutes ago you were very careful with this witness to ask him to distinguish between what he knew from his own knowledge and what he knew from what people told him. Why are you asking this witness to circle something which he has said quite clearly is not from his own knowledge, because he was not out of the prison during the war, and only what he believes to be the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand your objection, Your Honour. And with your leave, I will explain why. In his yesterday's testimony, the witness said that the front line, manned by the Vinko Skrobo unit, was about 400 metres long, and I wanted the witness to tell us which 400 metres, which area did he have in mind, so that in my defence I could then move on to prove where the front line was in reality. That is, I simply wanted to check his yesterday's statement that it was 400 metres. But if you think this is not necessary, that will be all right with me and I will move on to something else, because actually I have no other questions in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, I don't want to interrupt your cross-examination. I was just wondering, because you made such a distinction between hearsay and actual knowledge, why you were asking him to indicate on the map, because the witness has said that he didn't really know, it's just from what he heard from other people. But if you think it's important, please don't let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that -- at least as far as I'm concerned, I've clarified that point, but I can ask a specific question.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness U, yesterday, when you said that Vinko Skrobo, ATG, went some 400 metres over the separation line, would it be roughly the area that you pointed at? Do you think it is about 400 metres and a little bit more to the South, but you can see it on this photograph, another 100 metres or so towards the church. You cannot see it here because this is only part of the area shown here.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. And this is the information that you learned from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Absolutely so. I did not see any of this.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. All the knowledge that you have about the Vinko Skrobo unit regarding its strength, its tasks, its possible tasks, is all that information something that you learned from -- that you learned second-hand, something that is not your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm coming to the end of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, please, during your detention at Heliodrom, did your family -- was your family abreast of what was happening to you? Did they know whether you were dead or alive or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: What family do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I mean your family, the family that you live with, your next of kin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: My wife and my son did not know whether I was dead or alive, and my brothers were in the camp with me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, would that hold true of other prisoners, and was that the routine situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Don't ask me that. I really cannot speak on behalf of the whole camp. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to what you can tell us about yourself. Did, perhaps, your family get some hearsay, hear some rumours, about what had happened to you? Did they get any information? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Sir, you seem not to have been in this courtroom yesterday. I told you that my wife and my son went to Serbia in the early days of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not want to have any problem with the witness, so that I should like to thank you. This is the end of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for Witness U.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, in the beginning of your testimony, you spoke about your first arrest, your brothers' and your arrest in your apartment, and armed men who came, who then conducted searches saying that they were looking for weapons in your house. Did they find any weapons in your house at the time of your arrest? If they did not, under what pretext did they arrest you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: They found absolutely no weapons, nor did I ever have any weapons. I was a civilian until I returned from the camp. And my brother, who was an HVO member, had to leave his weapon with the unit. And the reason they took me away was because I was a Bosniak. They did not take any Croats away for such reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving us the evidence. We all wish you good luck. And the usher will show you out of the room once he pulls the blinds down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for your patience and understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any documents you would like to tender, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would like to tender Exhibit P11.18/2. That's the only document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no documents to tender, and I have no objections to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document is tendered into evidence. Madam Registrar will give a proper number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit is now numbered PP11.18/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So who will deal with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will deal with the next witness, and I think we should discuss some issues relevant to this witness. When our next witness, who is to be called to testify now, arrived here, he told us that he did not need any specific protective measures. But the only one, his full name not to be pronounced in the courtroom. He would rather -- he would prefer to be called in the courtroom by his first name. It's just something unusual, I know, in the practice of the Tribunal. But that was his desire, because he considers that his first name may be considered as a sort of pseudonym. But I know that there is a special procedure here for giving pseudonyms to witnesses. So I leave it at your discretion to decide. Anyway, I have prepared two documents, two papers, relevant to this witness, whether it will be Witness W, if you give him our traditional pseudonym, or his unusual pseudonym, Salko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you explain to him the difference between the pseudonym and the first name?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did my best. I did my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think according to the practice of this Tribunal, we better use a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and I would like to explain everything to the witness when he appears here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as before, no objections. We comply with every decision that you make, and we also accept -- go along with all the wishes of our learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we could bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that now we should discuss this problem in the presence of our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to discuss one problem with you. On your arrival here in The Hague, you stated that you wouldn't like your full name to be known in the courtroom, to be known to the public. And your preference was to be called in the courtroom by your first name. Just before you came here in this courtroom, this problem was discussed with the Trial Chamber, and I am authorised to inform you that according to the practice that exists here in the Tribunal, of the Tribunal, in such situations, witnesses are given a pseudonym for better protection of your identity during the trial. And the pseudonym that will be given to you is in alphabetical order, Witness W. So in this way you will be called in the courtroom "Witness W." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: I do not. I thought it could be done the way I suggested. If not, then let it be my full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean that you need not any protection? Would you like to testify in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphones of the witness are both switched off. We could not hear his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Would you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes, I want to testify publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Then I think there should be made some preparations in the courtroom now for the open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If this is your wish, we will use your full name, and the trial will be conducted in the open session. Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So, Witness, your full name, your first name, your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: My name is Salko Osmic. I was born near Prozor on the 10th of August, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any military background in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: No, except the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, doing my military service with it. Everybody -- that is, every young man had to serve it, and that was all. Nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long did your act of service in the Yugoslav army last?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: It lasted one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you live in Prozor municipality all the time? I mean before the war, I mean the war -- 1991, let's say.

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, yes, I only lived in Prozor, nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I don't think that it's necessary to give the name or the precise place where you lived. Was it just a town or a village?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: A village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever leave Prozor municipality for a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes. For a while, I worked in Croatia, for about eight months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: In 1987 or '88. I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you leave Prozor during the wartime, I mean from 1991, let's say, up to 1993?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question. Going where?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay, I will repeat or rephrase. Did you leave Prozor for some other locality in the period between '91 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Do you mean only Bosnia, or do you mean my moving elsewhere in Bosnia, perhaps going to Croatia or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, I did go up to Jablanica, Konjic, Vakuf. That would be the range, and those are all nearby towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I don't mean for short visits, but some longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever stay in Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, no, it was a nearby town, and only for a day or maybe two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What was happening in Prozor municipality in the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, please? Could you phrase your question more precisely, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, why don't you ask directly by, "What did you do during the war," or some question like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We have not come up to it yet. But if you would like to make it shorter, I can do that, I can do that. I wouldn't like, sorry, beating about the bush.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Precisely what were you doing during November 1992 in your village where you lived during the period of time where there were some military operations in the territory of Prozor municipality?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: At the beginning of the aggression again the B and H, I joined voluntarily the Territorial Defence, the TO. And then we went to the lines, to the front lines, and we worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was it a professional military unit?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: I cannot really say, explain. I think it was something like that. It was a joint army of Muslims and Croats under the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And was it still a mixed unit in November -- in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And you just told in your testimony something about aggression. Which aggression do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, I mean the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened in your village later in the fall of 1992, before you left it?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, when the HVO attacked Prozor, we remained at home. There were some attacks against us. But then things calmed down until the HVO attack began on Jablanica, and then I remained home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And when did the HVO attack Prozor?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: I think it was in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you participate in the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: An old M-48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You just told that at some period of time in April '93, you moved to Sovici. Did you keep your weapons and take it with you?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes, I took my weapons with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why did you move to that area?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You just told that there was some attack that was launched in Jablanica. So for some period of time you stayed at home, and then you moved to the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, the attack against Jablanica began on April 15th and the attack against Sovici on the 17th. So when the attack started against Jablanica, several of us, to see -- wanted to see what was going on there and to help the people there, and that is why we went to Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you report to any military command, on your arrival to Sovici, on your purposes and on yourself?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes, we reported to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many people were together with you? You are talking about some people, as I understand from your testimony, "we." How many people were there with you?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: There were five of us, five of us, five people with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you admitted to the military formation that was deployed in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes. We were deployed on some guard posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask you to just move to a private session for a short period of time, because the witness can give a name of some people whose names should be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What exactly was your assignment within that military formation?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, what we did was we were actually the village guard. We guarded the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: From the commander whose name I mentioned. We defended the village against the people in there who were Croats and the foreign army that had come there to attack the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any military units, other than Armija units in the area of Sovici at the time when you came to that village?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I didn't see it. But some people did, and they spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did your formation have?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: It was light weapons. We had two mortars and a PAM, double barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know more or less the geography of Sovici and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, a little. Some places I saw for the very first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where did you spend your shift on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, in the village. I was on guard in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: In the village itself?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes, in the village itself, 20 metres -- about 20 metres from the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did the military actions in Sovici begin?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: They started on April 17th, 'round about 8.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: In which location were you at that time, at the moment when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: On April 16th in the evening, we went out up to a hill where there was a defence; and on April 17th, I was there on the front lines of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see the beginning of the attack?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: As far as the beginning of the attack is concerned, it started by the shelling of the village, and then there was an infantry attack that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: From where was the shelling coming to the village?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, the village was totally encircled -- rather, from three sides. And at the time, I was on a hill, and the village was below. So I couldn't see very well. But they were basically from the direction of Blidinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was it possible to observe from the hill what exactly was happening during the attack in the village itself?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, what one could see more clearly was the attack by the tanks, the destruction of the houses, and the stalls. This could be seen more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what about your group of military during that attack? Did you put up any resistance?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, we did resist with what we had at our disposal, and we didn't have much. Five people were killed on that occasion. And at 2.00 p.m. in the afternoon, we left our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And which unit was involved in the attack on Sovici on your unit, on AbiH forces?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who attacked you? Who attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: I was not informed who took part in the attack; but afterwards, when I was arrested, I found out that Tuta's units was involved, the KB, the Convicts' Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would ask you -- just we will talk about some specific units further, but now I would like to -- did you see the soldiers who were attacking the village?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, I saw, but from afar. I couldn't really see which formations were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: To which army did they belong?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, of course, they belonged to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you leave the place where you were having your assignment with your weapons?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Yes, we left our positions with our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long did that attack last?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: From 8.00 a.m. to about 2.00 p.m., as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And did you observe from the hills what was happening in the village after it was secured by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, when the retreat from the lines took place, we approached the village. And there was general panic there, people crying, shouting, and that was the atmosphere. The village was placed under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any houses in the village destroyed at that time?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that then. We -- we saw that when we were on the -- up on the hill, we saw the tanks hit the buildings, the houses. But when we got down, it was dark already after some time, and then we went towards Jablanica. And after that, we saw nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And why did you go in the direction of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why did you go with the rest of your unit in the direction of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, the -- the rest of our unit was there. At the beginning, there were four or five. Of course we were going to the free territory, that's why we went to Jablanica, to avoid being killed by the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please don't talk into the microphone, because if you are too close to the microphone, there may be some interferences. Just you should be close enough, but not too close to the microphone. Okay?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you manage to join -- I'm sorry. Did you reach Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we did not succeed in reaching Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why? What happened?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: There was a lot of Croatian army around who blocked all the entry points towards Jablanica, and then we were trapped by them and then arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many soldiers were arrested together with you?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: There were about seven, including myself, and two minors. Nine, all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who were the people who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: We went to -- towards the people who were living there and belonged to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where does it take you after you had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: In the direction of Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you say -- I mean these local soldiers explained to you where you were to be taken?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: As regards the local soldiers, they were also very much under strong control and command, and they were afraid of the army also, but a little less than us. It was only when we went down to the command there, then Tuta and his soldiers directed us to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Let's expand a little bit on the command. What do you understand by "the command"?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: This is a meeting point where they took us, where the main commander, Tuta, was, and the rest of the army that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers there other than local soldiers from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Salko Osmic.
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. There were quite a number of those outside soldiers who were a little different from the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, now the time for the break is coming up, and I've got some more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we'll adjourn at this moment. We'll resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning. Oh, sorry. We'll resume at 2.00 in the afternoon. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
